classification.difficultyReason: Requires an unscaffolded proof strategy: add useful radii and chords, exploit BP=BC to constrain angles, and connect tangent geometry with angle bisection or equivalent length relations to prove OP=OQ.

content.prompt:
The circle centred at $O$ has diameter $AB$. A point $P$ on $AB$ produced is chosen so that $PC$ is a tangent to the circle at $C$ and $BP=BC$. The tangents to the circle at $A$ and $C$ meet at $Q$.

Prove that $OP=OQ$.

spec.description: Circle, diameter PBOA, tangent PCQ, tangent AQ extended beyond A, and chord BC with matching double ticks on BP and BC.
spec.mathematics: AB is a diameter, PC and QA are tangents, BP=BC. Coordinates express the exact compatible geometry without printing extra measurements.
spec.answerVisibility: OC, AC, OQ, derived equality marks and angle labels are withheld from the student figure.

answer.short: $\angle OPQ=\angle OQP=30^\circ$, so $\triangle OPQ$ is isosceles and $OP=OQ$.
answer.worked:
Construct $OC$, $AC$ and $OQ$. Let $\angle BPC=\phi$.

Since $BP=BC$, $\triangle BPC$ is isosceles, so $\angle BCP=\phi$. The exterior angle at $B$ gives $\angle OBC=2\phi$.

By the alternate segment theorem, $\angle BAC=\angle BCP=\phi$. Since $AB$ is a diameter, $\angle BCA=90^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\phi+2\phi&=90^\circ\\\phi&=30^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The radius is perpendicular to the tangent, so $OA\perp AQ$ and
$$\angle CAQ=90^\circ-\phi=60^\circ.$$
Tangents from $Q$ are equal: $QA=QC$. Thus $\triangle QAC$ is isosceles and $\angle QCA=60^\circ$. Hence
$$\angle AQC=180^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ=60^\circ.$$
Triangles $OAQ$ and $OCQ$ are congruent by SSS: $OA=OC$ (radii), $AQ=CQ$ (equal tangents), and $OQ$ is common. Therefore $OQ$ bisects $\angle AQC$, giving
$$\angle OQC=\frac{60^\circ}{2}=30^\circ=\angle OPC.$$
Since $P,C,Q$ are collinear, $\angle OQP=\angle OQC$ and $\angle OPQ=\angle OPC$. Thus $\triangle OPQ$ is isosceles and $OP=OQ$.
